source_evidence.anchor: opening matrix setting and column notation
source_evidence.observation: The standing setting is A in R^{m x n}, m >= n, rank(A)=n, with A=(a1,...,an), Q=(q1,...,qn), and R=(r_jk). In exact arithmetic the factorization has A=QR, Q^T Q=I_n, and upper-triangular nonsingular R.
Algorithm 2 (CGS-P) begins with r11=||a1||_2, q1=a1/r11, R1=(r11), and Q1=(q1).

The paper assumes IEEE floating-point arithmetic, states fl(x+y)=(x+y)(1+delta), |delta|<=epsilon_M for normalized-range results, and uses the first-order approximation (1+epsilon_M)^{p(n)}=1+p(n)epsilon_M+O(epsilon_M^2), treating the O(epsilon_M^2) contribution as insignificant.

Theorem 1 concerns the computed R and Q from Algorithm 2 and assumes c4(m,k) epsilon_M kappa_2(Rk)^2<1 for every k, where kappa_2(Rk)=||Rk||_2||Rk^{-1}||_2. Its residual conclusion is QkRk-Ak=Delta Ak with ||Delta Ak||_2<=c1(m,k)||Ak||_2 epsilon_M, to within O(epsilon_M^2), and c1(m,1)=1.

source_evidence.anchor: Remark 2, Algorithm 2 breakdown when assumptions fail
source_evidence.observation: The paper notes that without the assumptions of Theorem 1, phi_k can be at least psi_k and Algorithm 2 can break down, producing Q and R that are not real matrices.
Using condition (3), the proof concludes that R is nonsingular and hence every computed diagonal r_kk is positive.

source_evidence.observation: For the k=1 base case, standard error bounds give q1=(I+G1)a1/r11 with ||G1||_2<=epsilon_M.

source_evidence.observation: The proof then states the exact identity A1-Q1R1=a1-q1 r11=-G1 a1.
